headline: Past 18 months have seen lenders chasing returns without adequately understanding the underlying risks; investors need independent risk assessment benchmarked to bank-grade standards
reasoning: Craig flags that a key problem in recent private credit allocations has been a focus on headline yield without a commensurate understanding of the risk being taken to generate those returns. He contrasts this with Aura Group's approach of having its portfolio independently assessed against bank-grade standards monthly. He expects forthcoming disclosure requirements to give investors the tools to make more educated comparisons across managers.
quote: I think what we've seen in the past 18 months has been a very heavy focus on returns without the risk being taken to drive those returns. So as a manager, you know, we get our our portfolio independently assessed from a risk perspective every single month and using a long standing set of bank data, bank grade standards. In looking, looking at our risk, I think investors need to understand the risks that they're taking for the return that's being derived and more. So we'll see a lot of those disclosures coming out wherein investors will be able to make educated decisions on what they're going into.
episode_title: The private credit risks hiding behind the yield

headline: Increased ASIC regulation and disclosure standards will make private credit more robust, giving investors greater confidence in a nascent market
reasoning: ASIC has been conducting reviews of the retail private credit sector and is now focusing on the wholesale sector, with findings expected later in the year. Craig believes stronger and more consistent disclosures will help investors distinguish high-quality providers from unscrupulous operators that entered the market post-COVID. He argues that regulatory clarity will make the sector more robust and raise investor confidence in a market he still characterises as fairly nascent in Australia.
quote: ASIC have been doing a lot of report around, sorry, a lot of work around reporting standards for the broader industry. So they did a review into the retail private credit sector last year. This year they're focusing on the wholesale sector. Ultimately, we want strong transparency for investors there. We want to ensure that there's consistency across the disclosures. So ASIC will bring out their findings later on this year and we'll get a bit of guidance on what the regulator wants to see with a lot of those disclosures.
episode_title: The private credit risks hiding behind the yield

headline: Broader private credit market is generally healthy; Baffler collapse is an isolated case driven by heavy leverage and no bank funding, not a systemic warning sign
reasoning: Brett Craig argues the private credit market as a whole is in good shape. The Baffler situation is characterised as a heavily leveraged property development firm with no bank funding, which has been deteriorating for over 18 months as lenders offloaded exposure. He notes there is reportedly around $5 billion in assets backing $3.2-3.5 billion in loans, suggesting meaningful asset coverage. He also points out that among the 40+ private credit lenders in the transactions, outcomes will vary significantly depending on seniority, asset quality, valuations, and covenant protections.
quote: Bathler is one of those scenarios where you had a very heavily leveraged property development firm with no bank funding in there. We, we this has been an issue for over 18 months now where we saw a lot of lenders offloading exposure last year and then it's become a bit of a last man standing. One thing that we really haven't seen reported well in market is the actual asset backing on a lot of the loans that Baffa have there. So we've seen one report last week that that stated there were about $5 billion worth of assets against the circuit, 3.2 to $3.5 billion worth of loans.
episode_title: The private credit risks hiding behind the yield

headline: Risk-off macro environment with elevated long-end bond yields and soft economic feel despite positive GDP print; private assets held up well as a diversifier during COVID-style risk-off episodes
reasoning: Craig observes that despite a positive GDP print, the market feels relatively soft and long-end bond yields are at fairly elevated levels, signalling a risk-off environment. He draws on the COVID episode as a precedent where the traditional bond-equity correlation broke down, but high-quality private assets proved to be a good place to park capital. This positions private credit as a potential diversifier in the current environment relative to cash or listed income.
quote: Well, I think ultimately we we saw a pretty positive GDP prints day, but the market does feel relatively soft out there. Bond yields are moving at the long end to to fairly elevated levels that would suggest that it's, it's a pretty risk off market. What we did see throughout COVID, which was one of the more recent episodes of of risk off was that the correlations really broke down between bonds and equities and private assets was were high quality. Private assets were a good place to to park capital.

headline: Aura Group sees Australian property market entering a new phase with elevated investor nervousness and evaporating confidence amid policy and rate changes.
reasoning: Stanley Hsieh observes that the property market is undergoing both a cyclical and structural shift, driven by rising rates, rising construction costs, and new government budget policy pushing capital toward new builds. He notes that confidence in the broader market has evaporated, with many investors in a wait-and-see mode pending further policy details. Redemption requests are increasing across peer funds, signalling genuine investor concern. He nonetheless maintains that the fundamental case for lending to property and the need for new housing supply remains sound.
quote: I feel we've entered into a new property market, into a new phase of the property market... I do feel investors are generally quite nervous. We've already seen redemption requests in other a lot of my colleagues funds becoming an issue. So I think investors are rightly worried about what's happening to the property market. I really think the fundamental of the property market is still sound, and lending to property is still sound. The country still needs a lot of new supply coming on board.
episode_title: Nervous money flees complex property as Aura backs simple builds

headline: Australian budget policy structurally redirecting capital toward new residential builds, though developer confidence remains low pending policy detail.
reasoning: Hsieh highlights that the recent federal budget introduced a structural shift in the property market, with policy now explicitly pushing capital into new builds. However, many developers remain in limbo because detailed implementation of the policy has yet to be released. While Hsieh has seen renewed interest from developers responding to the policy direction, broader market confidence has evaporated in the near term as participants wait for clarity before committing to new projects.
quote: The policy is now pushing capital into new build. And, uh, a lot of details are still to come out. But in this flux of the market at the moment, there's just a lot of uncertainty... I've seen a lot of interest in developers moving again because that's where the policy is trying to encourage. But at the moment right now, a lot of them are still stuck in limbo because a lot of the policy details are still to come out. And I think generally the confidence around the market has evaporated for a while for the time being.
episode_title: Nervous money flees complex property as Aura backs simple builds

headline: Aura Group warns apartment and complex construction projects face severe feasibility challenges as property prices fall and costs rise, making equity buffers inadequate.
reasoning: Hsieh argues that complex projects such as apartment towers are disproportionately exposed to cost overruns because a fixed equity contribution can only absorb a smaller percentage increase in a large development cost. Operational complexity adds further risk — for example, replacing a builder mid-construction on a tower involves building commissioner defect reports and regulatory complications that make resolution extremely difficult. He notes that with property prices now falling and construction costs continuing to rise, feasibility for apartment developments is very challenged, compressing margins further for developers.
quote: When you have an apartment building, you know, a builder fell in halfway through a construction and you have to replace a builder in a tower. The regulator building commissioner defects reports and so on makes these projects really, really difficult to work out. And those creates complications and complexity I talk about that could potentially lead to trouble... I see feasibility being very challenged, especially now that property prices are coming down, costs continue to go up. That's the example where your million dollar equity will have to buffer a big development cost relative to your equity.
episode_title: Nervous money flees complex property as Aura backs simple builds

headline: Aura Group favours simple residential builds — houses, duplexes, triplexes, and subdivisions — as a resilient segment that can absorb cost overruns and deliver real housing supply.
reasoning: Hsieh explains that simpler projects such as house builds, duplexes, triplexes, and land subdivisions have a much better equity-to-development-cost ratio, allowing a fixed equity contribution to absorb proportionally larger construction cost blowouts. Aura's own funds are focused on this segment — with live projects including duplexes in Castle Hill, Bondi, and Bronte — and are performing well. He argues this is also the segment that will genuinely bring new supply to the market, aligning with government policy intent. Complexity in financial structuring and project type is the key risk indicator Hsieh uses to screen borrowers.
quote: We focus on length, subdivision, simple house build, duplex, triplex. We've got projects in Castlehill. That's a duplex in Bondi, Bronte that's a duplex, and so on. I think this segment of the market will continue to perform well because they that is the segment of the market that will bring real supply to the market... In Aura we focus on the smaller projects where your $1 million equity can buffer 2 or 3 times crossover around in the construction and still be okay.
episode_title: Nervous money flees complex property as Aura backs simple builds

headline: High-quality, low-leverage private credit yield products seeing strong investor demand amid CGT changes shifting capital from equities
reasoning: Craig notes that recent changes to CGT provisions in the budget have made capital account assets taxed in line with income, prompting investors to rotate toward yield-generating assets. High-quality yield products in private credit continue to attract strong demand as a result. He emphasises that quality is the key differentiator — high-quality businesses that are not overleveraged can still provide attractive yield even through a downturn. Investors are increasingly looking at yield products as an alternative to equities.
quote: It all comes down to quality. The reality is, even in a downturn in a cycle, high quality businesses who are not overleveraged and are looking at, um, borrowing responsibly at low leverage levels will still provide a really good source of yield for investors... with the changes to CGT provisions in the recent budget. Investors are now looking at assets that sit on capital account being treated in line with income accounts. So we've seen strong demand for for yield assets. Um, what it really comes down to is the investor ensuring that they're going into to a quality provider and understanding what's, you know, in that product. So high quality yield products are still seeing strong demand. And I think that, you know, investors are starting to look at yield products as opposed to to equities.
episode_title: A cautious, yet constructive view on Aussie private credit

headline: Australian small businesses and consumers face a tough environment as rate rises, budget impacts, and falling property prices weigh on confidence and demand
reasoning: Craig warns that interest rate rises have begun to bite and budget impacts have flowed through the market over the past two months, creating a negative wealth effect for consumers. Falling property prices are weakening consumer balance sheets, leading to drops in discretionary income and consumer confidence. While unemployment remains relatively resilient, he sees an inflection point ahead where businesses facing rising insurance costs and interest rates will be forced to stop hiring or cut staff. This creates a difficult environment for small business borrowers in particular.
quote: I think we're in for a tough time in the Australian market. The reality is interest rate rises have started to to bite, and we've probably seen more impact from that budget flowing through the market in the last two months. The reality is consumers are feeling a negative wealth effect. So we're starting to see those property prices dropping. The consumer's balance sheet is is is waning. So as a result we'll start to see consumer confidence dropping obviously are the discretionary incomes dropping. Unemployment is holding up there quite well at this point in time. However there will be an inflection point when businesses who are feeling that cost pressure with rising insurance costs, interest rates going up, They will have to either stop looking for new employees as the demand is not there, or look at culling their existing set.
episode_title: A cautious, yet constructive view on Aussie private credit

headline: Brett Craig flags highly leveraged construction as one of the highest-risk areas in Australian private credit to avoid

He cites a recent example of a large western Sydney property developer (Baffler) with approximately $3 billion in financing but only around $30 million in net equity on balance sheet, illustrating how thin equity buffers become dangerous in a rising cost and rising interest rate environment. He advises investors to steer clear of these sectors.
quote: What you really need to see clear of, in my view, is, is any of those distressed assets also highly leveraged construction. I think there are two of the areas where we see some significant risk. Is that likely to get worse? Do you think when you talk about a highly leveraged construction, um, what are you seeing at the moment? Uh, I mean, in the press recently, we've seen a group under some strain baffler. So a large western Sydney property developer, where they do have quite a bit of financing in their circa $3 billion, with about $30 million sitting on balance sheet in net equity. So looking at that kind of dynamic, it doesn't play out that well in a rising cost and rising interest rate environment.
episode_title: A cautious, yet constructive view on Aussie private credit

headline: Australian private credit market more resilient than US due to hard-asset collateral and lower leverage, but faces domestic headwinds
reasoning: Brett Craig argues the Australian private credit market is at a more nascent stage than the US and predominantly lends against hard assets with lower leverage, making it more robust. By contrast, the US market has significant exposure to PE-backed deals and SaaS businesses where collateral is forward cash flows, which is where stress is emerging. In Australia, the primary risks are concentrated in the construction sector, where feasibility of projects is being challenged by falling property prices and rising costs. He notes South Australia has recently joined states with negative property price growth, adding to concerns about the construction pipeline.
quote: The reality is the Australian market is in a much more nascent stage than the US market. And a lot of the lending that's being done in the Australian market is against hard assets, whereas in the US there are a lot of deals where private equity buyers are coming in and private credit are providing the leverage to those PE firms. We've got a lot of SaaS funding that's being done. So funding to software as a service, businesses where the collateral that's backing those loans is the Ford cash flows. And I think where some of the real issues lies when those Ford cash cash flows are compromised. That's probably what we've seen in in that US space in Australia. Some of the risks are primarily, as ASIC and APRA have noted, in that construction sector, where you're seeing house prices, property prices generally dropping post the budget.
episode_title: A cautious, yet constructive view on Aussie private credit
